howto.text: Be at least 18 with a high school diploma or equivalent and a U.S. Social Security number.

howto.name: Complete the 63-hour pre-license course
howto.text: Finish Florida's state-approved 63-hour sales associate pre-license course and pass its end-of-course exam.

howto.name: Get fingerprinted
howto.text: Submit electronic fingerprints through a state-approved vendor for your background check.

howto.name: Apply to the DBPR
howto.text: Apply to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and receive your exam authorization.

howto.name: Pass the Florida state exam
howto.text: Pass the 100-question Florida sales associate exam (75% or higher) at a Pearson VUE testing center.

howto.text: Join a licensed Florida broker, such as Adams, Cameron & Co., to activate your license and start working.

Daytona Beach Shores is a small, dense barrier-island town of about 5,200 people, directly on the Atlantic and sandwiched between Daytona Beach and Ponce Inlet. It's made up largely of oceanfront condos, with a mix of year-round residents and seasonal or vacation-home owners. Here's exactly how to get licensed, and what this local market looks like for a new agent.

How do you get a real estate license in Daytona Beach Shores?

You earn the Florida real estate sales associate license, valid statewide. There is no separate Daytona Beach Shores license. Be 18+ with a high school diploma, complete the 63-hour pre-license course, get fingerprinted, apply to the DBPR, pass the state exam (75% to pass), and activate under a broker. Most people finish in two to four months. Full detail is in our Florida licensing guide.

Is Daytona Beach Shores a good market for a new real estate agent?

It's a genuine niche. Daytona Beach Shores is small, so it won't hand a new agent the sheer transaction volume of a larger city. What it offers instead is a concentrated, mostly-condo coastal market wedged between two much larger areas, Daytona Beach to the north and Ponce Inlet to the south, both of which a Daytona Beach Shores-based agent can also work. Condo sales, seasonal buyers, and vacation-home owners have their own rhythm and their own paperwork, so an agent who learns this stretch of barrier island well becomes genuinely useful to buyers and sellers who want someone who actually knows oceanfront condo living, not just the county median.

Daytona Beach Shores was founded in 1960 as a planned condo community

Daytona Beach Shores was incorporated in 1960 by moteliers known as the “2,000 Cottages,” intentionally built to provide better services than Daytona Beach to the north. Today, roughly 90% of Daytona Beach Shores lives in high-rise condominiums. Two major construction booms (1970s–1980s and early 2000s) left a legacy of modern oceanfront towers with planned amenities. For a new agent, this concentration is not a weakness: it’s clarity. You’re not competing in a general market; you’re working in a condo-first barrier island city where buyers expect expertise in oceanfront high-rise living.

Seasonal residents and vacation-home buyers: half the population is part-time

Roughly half of Daytona Beach Shores sits vacant during off-season months. The city has a dense population of seasonal residents, snowbirds, and rental investors. For an agent, it means understanding buyers that mainland agents rarely work with: the couple escaping northern winters, the investor calculating rental revenue, the retiree wanting oceanfront without year-round commitment. These buyers negotiate differently. They need an agent who understands the seasonal rhythm, rental income potential, and capital-gains implications of part-time ownership.

HOA fees and coastal property maintenance: understanding the real costs

Daytona Beach Shores has 87 registered communities with monthly HOA fees from $400 to over $900. Oceanfront properties face salt-air corrosion, higher insurance premiums, and ongoing structural work (elevator modernization, roof replacement, foundation repair). Buyers need an agent who can read an HOA budget and explain why a 30-year-old oceanfront condo costs more to maintain than an inland house. Agents who can walk a buyer through an HOA reserve fund study will win deals that competitors miss.

The investor and rental market in a condo-first city

Daytona Beach Shores is one of the most investor-friendly barrier-island markets in Volusia County, with much of the seasonal vacancy driven by short-term rental investors. An investor comparing a $450K oceanfront condo against rental revenue is making a different transaction than a retiree seeking a winter place. They need comps and rental data, not neighborhood charm. They need an agent who knows that a flexible HOA policy is worth more than an identical property with rental restrictions. Knowing this market means knowing the numbers.

Does the brokerage you start with matter?

More than the town you pick. Your license must be held by a broker, and that brokerage decides your training, tools, and support in the make-or-break first year. A recognized local name carries real weight, and sellers trust it before you say a word, which matters even more in a small, tight-knit coastal community where reputations travel fast.

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the area's largest brokerage since 1963, with around 300 agents and offices across Volusia and Flagler County, including its headquarters just up the coast at 600 S. Atlantic Ave in Daytona Beach. New agents get in-house marketing at no cost, seven-day non-competing manager support, structured training, and the global Leading Real Estate Companies of the World referral network.

What is your next step?

Read the licensing guide, go deeper on the town’s real story in our full history of Daytona Beach Shores, then start a conversation with Adams, Cameron & Co. No pressure, just a clear picture of the path.
